title: The Bramblefly, the Double B, and the Way Home: A Sequel to The Soul-Ring, the Feywild Wildfire, and the Twenty-One Day Cut
subtitle: In Which Waluigi Reads the Minutes, Defends His Own Bias, and Refuses to Invent the Missing Frame
filed: 23 October 2026 — desk reading of the session notes; not a Feyward clock time
pullQuote: Waluigi would love the missing frame to show a perfect spell, a defeated Bramblefly, and a signed route home. The notes show none of those. WAH!
standfirst: The conceit is a live reading of the session notes at Waluigi’s desk: he pauses at every gap, heckles his own wishful thinking, and lets the paper stop where the event stops. This is not recovered camera footage. The Double B’s operator and destination remain unknown; Waluigi is reading the notes, not claiming the recording.

sections.heading: EIGHT AND A HALF HOURS IS NOT A CLOCK
sections.body:
The desk lamp is on, the notes are under Waluigi’s left hand, and the performance begins with the only duration that survives intact: eight and a half hours. The page says, “The interval is the firmest clock evidence in the notes; it is not a claim that every person slept for all of it.” Waluigi reads that twice, because the temptation to turn a duration into a sunrise is very strong and sunrise is very pretty and WRONG. The carried-forward time anchor is itself an estimate around 05:00. Add the stated rest and you get an estimated 13:30. You do not get a bell, a chime, or a witness pointing at a clock. WAH!

Waluigi is already biased toward a clock when a clock would make the page look finished. Waluigi likes headings, dates, and tidy margins; the Feyward has spent this whole campaign making those preferences look like a personal defect. So the time stays an estimate. The rest is real; the precision is not. That is not a weakness in the account. It is the part of the account Waluigi trusts most.

The card-room deadline sits in the background, but Waluigi does not let that deadline turn into a countdown montage. The group rests. That is the beat. The notes do not say everyone sleeps, the notes do not say the manor becomes safe, and the notes do not say the clock pauses because the party is tired. Waluigi reads the plain sentence, looks at the empty margin where a minute-by-minute schedule would go, and refuses to draw one in. AWAKE, asleep, waiting, listening—only the named actions go on the page. Waluigi is not letting suspense write its own timesheet.

NO dawn, NO bell, NO clock face—only a rest interval and arithmetic. Waluigi can add; he cannot magically upgrade an estimate. THAT is the line.

And NO, an estimate is NOT a sunrise just because the paragraph wants one.

sections.heading: A SECURED ROOM, THEN SIX HOURS
sections.body:
The next line on the page is short: “Hjumpik secured the room before sleeping.” Then: “He then slept for six hours.” Waluigi taps the desk at that second sentence. Six hours is a proper rest, not a dramatic montage in which the dwarf somehow patrols every corridor, checks every window, and also dreams in three acts. The notes say he secured the room and slept. That is what happened here.

Waluigi’s own task is the paperwork. The contents are not named, and that omission is extremely annoying to an archivist who enjoys knowing what is in the folder. It is also not permission to invent a requisition, a report, or a list of supplies. Waluigi works; the paper’s subject remains unspecified. That is the boundary. WAH, a boundary! In a manor where even the rooms have had boundary issues, Waluigi finds this one reassuring.

There is a small bias in how Waluigi tells this beat. A secured room sounds like competence; paperwork sounds like Waluigi; sleeping sounds like the other person’s good sense. Naturally the cut wants to praise the parts that flatter Waluigi. But Hjumpik’s room security is the concrete preparation, and Hjumpik gets the six hours. Waluigi does not claim he stood watch, because these notes do not say that. He does not claim the room was impenetrable, because the notes do not say that either. He keeps the praise narrow: Hjumpik made the room safer, then rested. The party did not defeat the manor by closing a door. It got a pause, and the pause mattered.

A secured room is GOOD. A guaranteed room is NOT in these notes. Hjumpik gets the credit; the door gets no superhero cape.

GOOD preparation is not INVULNERABILITY; Waluigi can admire the lock without declaring the room IMPOSSIBLE to enter.

sections.heading: THE ROUTE HOME IS STILL AN ARGUMENT
sections.body:
The next heading is not “The Escape.” It is “The Route Home Is Not a Route Yet.” Waluigi reads the passage about the party debating how to get home and hears the gap between wanting an exit and having one. There is disagreement. There is planning. There is no departure and no agreed route. The notes do not identify every proposed path, so the cut does not invent a map with three arrows and a dotted line. Waluigi can draw a dotted line. Waluigi will not.

The Feyward deadline is in the background, which makes the debate feel urgent without resolving it. Waluigi would love to say that the party chose the most practical option, preferably the option that puts Waluigi somewhere with a normal floor and a door that stays a door. But a preference is not a vote. The argument remains a disagreement, and the clock remains an estimate moving forward. Everyone can be right that home matters and still be uncertain how to reach it. WAH, a rare occasion when wanting the same thing does not magically produce a route.

The bias here is obvious: Waluigi wants the discussion to end in a decision because indecision is uncomfortable and because Waluigi would like to be out of the Feywild. That does not mean the party’s disagreement was foolish. The manor is still dangerous; the camera has interrupted the plan; the Bramblefly remains ahead. A rushed answer could be worse than a pause. The notes do not tell us who argued for which route or who yielded, so Waluigi’s microphone captures no invented speeches. It captures the fact that they debated, did not settle it, and then the story moved into the Bowser-card beat.

A route is NOT a wish, a debate is NOT a vote, and wanting home is NOT the same as being there. Waluigi knows. Waluigi STILL wants it.

That is NOT a route. It is NOT settled. It is NOT suddenly simple because Waluigi says it LOUDER.

sections.heading: A CARD CHANGES HANDS; A ROUTE DOES NOT
sections.body:
Waluigi holds the page flat and reads the exact limitation: “A Bowser business card was exchanged while the party debated its way home.” The card matters because it was exchanged. It does not become a portal just because the party needs one. The notes give no printed wording, no exact hands, and no final keeper. Waluigi knows how to make a business card look like the beginning of a major arrangement; Waluigi also knows that a rectangle with a name on it is not a signed agreement. This is a conflict of interest. Waluigi likes business cards. Waluigi likes being contacted. Waluigi likes a route home even more.

The card can be a contact, a prompt, a token, or a piece of paper that changes hands and then sits in somebody’s pocket. Until its text and keeper are known, those remain possibilities, not findings. Waluigi would enjoy a Bowser arrangement that solved the transport problem. He would enjoy it so much that he has to say out loud that the notes do not establish one. WAH! See? Waluigi can be fair to evidence even when the evidence is shaped like an opportunity.

And no, this does not mean the exchange is meaningless. It changes what the group can do if the card remains accessible and if the contact can be reached. Those are two ifs. The card’s existence is a beat; its promise is not known. Waluigi does not turn it into a contract, does not announce that Bowser accepted responsibility, and does not pretend the card itself carries the group home. One object moved between people. The conversation stayed unsettled. Both facts fit on the same page without making the card more powerful than it is.

A card is NOT a portal, NOT a contract, NOT a ride, and NOT even a confirmed keeper. It is a card. Waluigi’s disappointment is REAL.

CONTACT is not COMMITMENT. Waluigi knows the difference; Waluigi merely dislikes it VERY much.

sections.heading: THE DOUBLE B INTERRUPTS THE PERFORMANCE
sections.body:
The notes say, “The party’s planning and movement were interrupted by a Double B camera and its recording.” Waluigi stops reading. This is the point where the desk performance becomes personally uncomfortable: Waluigi is narrating a recording interruption while the actual device’s operator and destination are unknown. The Double B camera is part of the scene. Whether anyone has the footage is not established. Nobody gets to point at a blank and say the camera sent its recording to the Legion. Waluigi would like to know who has it. Waluigi would like the camera to have a name tag, an address, and a return policy. It does not.

The Iron Legion logo is visible. That is useful. It connects the scene to the Legion’s presence, but it does not prove who owned the camera, who operated it, or whether the observers were at its controls. Waluigi distrusts the Legion, and Waluigi is very good at noticing the details that support his suspicion. That is precisely why this distinction matters: suspicion is a lens, not a photograph. The logo is a photograph-shaped fact; the attribution is still missing.

The notes do not state whether the recording was live, stored, recovered, erased, or passed to anyone. Waluigi cannot produce footage he never received. Waluigi cannot identify an unseen operator. He can say the camera interrupted the covert movement and made surveillance part of the scene. That is already enough to complicate the approach. A party trying not to be noticed has now noticed a device associated with recording. Waluigi lowers the page, peers at the ceiling as though there might be another lens, and then catches himself inventing one. No. One camera is the one the notes name. WAH!

LOGO: visible. OPERATOR: unknown. DESTINATION: unknown. Waluigi wants the whole picture; the notes give him one sharp corner.

A MARK is not a PERSON. A RECORDING is not a DELIVERY. Waluigi is not filling either gap with DRAMA.

sections.heading: QUIETLY DOES NOT MEAN UNSEEN
sections.body:
After the interruption, the party approaches the Bramblefly covertly. Waluigi reads the word “covertly” and circles it in the air with one finger. It describes an attempt and a posture; it does not certify success. The notes do not give a route, distance, or surprise result. This distinction irritates Waluigi because “the party tried to move quietly” sounds less impressive than “the party slipped past everyone,” and Waluigi is a professional admirer of impressive entrances. But the second sentence would be made up. We are staying with the first.

Quartermaster Cornburary’s observers are present in the account. Their count, names, positions, and orders are not. Waluigi has seen enough military paperwork to know that the word observer can cover a great deal of activity, but he does not know which activity happened here. He cannot turn unnamed watchers into a fully briefed squad, nor can he say that they saw everything. The camera and the observers may be connected; they may not be. Waluigi’s mind wants a single coordinated operation because a single operation is a clean diagram. The notes do not supply the connecting arrows.

The approach therefore carries two feelings at once: deliberate care and uncertain exposure. The party did not enter the encounter casually. It tried to choose its terms after a rest and a planning debate. Yet the camera has already interrupted the effort, and Cornburary’s observers sit in the same account without identified orders. Waluigi’s bias says the party should get credit for a good plan. Waluigi’s honesty says the record shows an attempt, not the outcome of the attempt. The Bramblefly is the destination; the success of concealment remains unproved. Quietly is what they tried. Unseen is what nobody established.

COVERT is the attempt. UNSEEN is not established. The distinction is SMALL on the page and HUGE in a corridor.

ATTEMPTED quietly does not mean SUCCESSFULLY hidden. The words are DIFFERENT for a reason.

sections.heading: A FIGHT IS NOT A FATE
sections.body:
The next sentence is plain: “The party fought the Bramblefly.” Waluigi can say that. The engagement happened. This is not another glimpse of the creature and not merely a retreat from its corridor; the notes identify a fight. What the notes do not preserve is the sequence: who struck first, who moved where, what resources were spent, what injuries were taken, or which action ended the encounter. Waluigi would love a full tactical replay. He would love to freeze the frame at the decisive moment and explain the excellent form of whichever action was his. The frame is missing. The pose is not available for admiration. WAH!

The outcome of a fight and the fate of its opponent are related, but they are not the same sentence. The encounter reached an end in the notes available here; the Bramblefly’s final status is not identified. Dead, driven off, captured, or still active are four different futures. Waluigi cannot choose one because it gives the next paragraph a cleaner landing. This fight does not come with a spare ending to borrow. Waluigi refuses the tempting shortcut.

This is where his ego gets in the way. Waluigi wants a battle to have a winner, preferably a winner who used magic with style and whose plan was obviously correct from the beginning. But the record does not make that offer. It gives the fight and collateral damage, then stops short of a creature’s fate. Waluigi can celebrate the party’s willingness to confront a continuing danger without writing that the threat is gone. The fight matters. The missing outcome matters too. Waluigi puts the microphone closer and reads the next line instead of supplying a victory speech.

Fight: YES. Fate: UNKNOWN. Waluigi wants the clean win; the record will not print one. NOT YET.

An ending is not a DISPOSITION. Waluigi wants one; Waluigi does not HAVE one.

sections.heading: THE MANOR GETS A BILL, NOT AN ADDRESS
sections.body:
“The fight caused collateral damage to the manor.” Waluigi reads that with the solemnity of a man who has seen a repair invoice arrive at the worst possible moment. The damage is real in the notes. Its location and extent are not. There is no named wall, floor, room, window, or object to point at. There is no estimate of cost, no repair schedule, and no survey that identifies whether the damage compounded an old break. The manor has taken a hit, but Waluigi cannot say which part of the building will complain first.

Waluigi’s first instinct is to make the damage vivid. A falling beam is vivid. A shattered balustrade is vivid. A hole punched through a floor is extremely vivid and would make a nice illustration. None of those details is in this account. Waluigi crosses them out before they become nouns. This is not restraint imposed by a supervisor. This is the annoying work of having standards while one’s imagination is fully stocked with dramatic architecture.

There is one thing Waluigi will concede, and it is physical: collateral damage to the manor is not a metaphor for the party’s feelings. Something in the place was damaged. That fact matters even without an address, because the manor is the ground the group still has to move through. But it does not let Waluigi declare a collapse or assign a repair bill. He looks at the blank space where the damaged feature should be named, then leaves it blank. The party has a physical consequence. The map of that consequence is still missing. WAH, a building can be injured without the archivist getting to decide where it hurts.

Damage: YES. Address: UNKNOWN. Extent: UNKNOWN. The manor has a bill; Waluigi does NOT get to choose the line items.

A consequence is not a MAP. Waluigi cannot point to a place the notes never NAME.

sections.heading: THE SPELL IS NOT IN THE MARGIN
sections.body:
The event says, “Waluigi used magic during the Bramblefly engagement.” That is the action the notes preserve. They do not identify a spell, target, visible effect, or result. Waluigi’s hand goes to the margin anyway. He has a long list of spells that would look magnificent beside a giant insect, and each one would make this paragraph much more satisfying. The list stays in his head. The story does not name the spell. Waluigi does not write one in.

There is a bias worth admitting: when Waluigi is the person using magic, Waluigi wants the magic to be central, effective, and elegantly timed. Those are flattering descriptions. They may even be true, but the supplied notes do not establish them. The only safe statement is that he used magic during the fight. The article’s XP preview is correspondingly modest about what it credits; the authoritative player total remains untouched until the table confirms it. Waluigi doesn’t get to use a spell he cannot identify to take credit for collateral he cannot locate against a creature whose fate is unknown. This is a very unfortunate arrangement for Waluigi and an excellent arrangement for truth.

The magic still belongs in the story. Leaving it out would erase a documented action merely because its mechanics were not carried forward. Waluigi can make the action visible while keeping its effect open. He can say the magic occurred and stop before naming its school, shape, or tactical value. WAH! It is possible to be present in a scene and still not know every detail of how it resolves. Waluigi is learning this. He dislikes it. He is learning it anyway.

Magic: YES. Named spell: NO. Target: NOT specified. Effect: NOT specified. Waluigi hates a blank that accurately describes him.

An action is not an EFFECT. Waluigi’s pride is not a source document. THIS is painful.

sections.heading: THE SCREENING STOPS WHERE THE NOTES STOP
sections.body:
Waluigi reaches the last section of the notes. The route home is unresolved. The card’s meaning and final keeper are unknown. The camera’s operator, footage destination, and custody are not established. Cornburary’s observers have no names or orders in the account. The Bramblefly fought the party, the manor took collateral damage, and Waluigi used magic; the creature’s final fate, the damage’s address, and the spell’s effect remain open. Waluigi reads each item slowly, because a list of open questions is not the same thing as an answer hiding in the punctuation.

The date can be carried forward only as an estimate: the approximate 05:00 anchor plus eight and a half hours gives about 13:30 on 3 Aethel. The deadline began at 01:30, so the display advances by twelve hours and leaves twenty days, twelve hours. Waluigi likes the arithmetic. Waluigi does not mistake arithmetic for a witnessed clock. The result inherits the original estimate, and the article says so.

The screen goes dark on a party that has rested, debated, exchanged a card, faced an interrupted covert approach, and fought the Bramblefly. There is no montage of everyone leaving the manor. There is no final shot of the insect. There is no camera operator stepping out from behind the leaves. Waluigi wants all three. The notes supply none. He closes the page, not the questions. WAH! Tomorrow’s desk can take up the part the table actually brings back.

Estimated is NOT witnessed. About is NOT exact. The countdown advances; it does NOT turn a calculation into a clock reading. WAH! The page does not say how long the fight or the discussion lasted, either. Waluigi cannot use the timecode as a stopwatch for each action. The screen fades on that limit, not on a made-up final minute.

The estimate is STILL an estimate. The count is DERIVED. Waluigi can show the math without pretending to have SEEN the clock.
